title: Ideas Unleashed: Reformation and Science
summary: In 1517 a monk named Martin Luther wrote ninety-five arguments, and printers copied them so fast that all of Germany was soon talking about them. Bibles in everyday languages, cartoons and science books with amazing pictures spread the same way. Rulers tried to ban books, but once hundreds of copies existed, ideas were very hard to stop.

sections.heading: A Monk, Ninety-five Arguments and a Printing Frenzy
paragraphs: Picture the small university town of Wittenberg, in Saxony in eastern Germany, in the autumn of 1517. It is not a great city like Venice or Paris. It has muddy streets, a castle, a church, a young university and a few thousand people. One of its teachers is a monk and professor of Bible studies named Martin Luther, a stocky, stubborn, brilliant man in his early thirties who has been growing more and more upset about something called indulgences.

An indulgence was a church certificate that, people were told, reduced the punishment for sins after death. In 1517 a preacher named Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences near Wittenberg to raise money, partly for rebuilding St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Luther thought this was wrong: forgiveness, he believed, could not be bought. So on 31 October 1517 he wrote a list of ninety-five short arguments in Latin, called theses, inviting other scholars to debate the question. We know he sent them in a letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz on that date.

You may have seen paintings of Luther angrily hammering the paper onto the wooden door of Wittenberg's Castle Church. That famous scene might have happened, because church doors were used like notice boards for university debates. But historians genuinely argue about it. The first written account of the hammering came from Luther's friend Philipp Melanchthon, who told it only after Luther died in 1546, and Melanchthon was not in Wittenberg in 1517. So the door story is possible, but not certain.

What IS certain is far more important for our story: the theses were printed, and they spread astonishingly fast. Before the end of 1517, printers in at least three cities, Leipzig, Nuremberg and Basel, had turned out their own editions. One was a large poster-style sheet that could be pinned up; another was a little four-page pamphlet you could slip into a bag. Soon they were translated into German so that people who did not read Latin could follow the argument too. Luther's friend Friedrich Myconius later wrote that within about four weeks almost all of Christendom seemed to know about them. That is an exaggeration, but it shows how it felt to people living through it.

Luther himself was surprised. In March 1518 he wrote that his theses had been printed and passed around far beyond what he had expected. He had meant to start a debate among professors. Instead, thanks to the printing press, he had started an argument with the whole of Europe.

Think about why this was new. A century earlier, other critics of the church, like Jan Hus in Bohemia, had also attracted followers. But their ideas travelled mostly by sermons and hand-copied writings, and they could be stamped out locally. In 1517 there were presses in more than 200 towns across Europe, run by businesspeople who needed to sell things. A hot argument that everyone was talking about was exactly what they wanted to print.

sections.heading: Pamphlets, Best-sellers and Picture Wars
paragraphs: Luther quickly discovered he was a natural writer for the new medium. Instead of long, heavy Latin books for scholars, he wrote short pamphlets in lively German, often just 8 or 16 pages. Germans called these little booklets Flugschriften, which means something like flying writings, because they flew from town to town. They were cheap to print, cheap to buy and quick to reprint. If a pamphlet sold out in Augsburg, a printer in Strasbourg could simply buy one copy, set it in type again and sell his own edition the following week.

His 1518 Sermon on Indulgence and Grace shows how this worked. It was reprinted about twenty times, by printers in Wittenberg, Leipzig, Nuremberg, Augsburg, Basel and other cities. The historian Andrew Pettegree, who has studied the numbers carefully, counts about 160 different works by Luther printed in about 828 editions by the end of 1522. Within five years of the theses, Luther had become the most published author Europe had ever seen. Historians estimate that his writings made up a very large share of everything printed in Germany in the early 1520s.

His side also simply outprinted their opponents. Between 1521 and 1525, Luther and his supporters published roughly nine times as much as the writers defending the old church. Part of the reason was business: printers printed what sold, whatever their own beliefs. Catholic replies were often long, written in Latin and harder to sell.

Germany's political map helped as well. The Holy Roman Empire was a patchwork of hundreds of separate territories and free cities, each with its own ruler. A book banned in one city could be printed just over the border in another. In 1521 Emperor Charles V outlawed Luther and banned his writings with the Edict of Worms, but in practice the ban was very hard to enforce, and Luther was hidden and protected by his own prince, Frederick the Wise of Saxony.

Many Germans could not read at all. Historians think only a small minority could read well, perhaps a few percent in the countryside and more in the towns. Yet pamphlets still reached them, because people read aloud. One literate person in a tavern, a market square or a family kitchen could share a pamphlet with dozens of listeners. Ideas also spread through songs printed on cheap sheets, which people sang to tunes they already knew.

Pictures were the other secret weapon. Woodcuts, the carved-wood pictures you met earlier in this Deep Dive, could be printed alongside text. The painter Lucas Cranach the Elder, who ran a busy workshop in Wittenberg, designed portraits of Luther and decorated the title pages of his works so that a Luther pamphlet had a recognizable look, a bit like a brand. In 1521 Cranach's workshop made the Passional Christi und Antichristi, a little book of paired pictures: on one page Jesus washes his followers' feet, and on the opposite page the pope has his own feet kissed. You did not need to read a word to understand the message.

The other side fought back with pictures too. In 1529 a woodcut published with a book by the Catholic writer Johannes Cochlaeus showed Luther as a monster with seven heads. These printed picture battles were early cousins of political cartoons. Both sides could be rude, unfair and exaggerated, which reminds us that print spreads insults and half-truths as easily as careful thinking.

sections.heading: Bibles for Ordinary Readers
paragraphs: In 1521, after refusing to take back his writings, Luther was secretly taken for his safety to the Wartburg, a castle on a forested hill in Thuringia. There he grew a beard, called himself Junker Jörg (Knight George) and set himself an enormous task: translating the New Testament from Greek into everyday German. He worked astonishingly fast, finishing a first version in about eleven weeks.

Luther wanted German that sounded like real people talking. He said he listened to mothers at home, children in the streets and ordinary people in the market to hear how they spoke. His translation was printed in Wittenberg in September 1522, so it is nicknamed the September Testament. It was printed in Melchior Lotter's shop with woodcut illustrations from Cranach's workshop, including dramatic pictures for the Book of Revelation. A first run of a few thousand copies, usually given as about 3,000, sold out within weeks, and a corrected edition appeared in December. Even so, it was not cheap: a full Bible was worth weeks of wages for a working person.

In 1534 the complete Luther Bible, Old Testament included, came off the press of Hans Lufft in Wittenberg, with 117 woodcuts. Over the following decades hundreds of thousands of copies of Luther's Bibles and New Testaments were printed. Because Germany had many dialects, his widely read translation also helped shape a common written German. It was not the only cause, but many language historians see it as a big step toward modern standard German.

In England, a scholar named William Tyndale had the same dream for English. At that time, translating the Bible into English without church permission was forbidden in England. Tyndale is said to have told a churchman that he would make a boy who drives the plough know more of the Scriptures than he did. Unable to get support at home, he went to Germany in 1524.

His first attempt to print, in Cologne in 1525, was discovered by an opponent and raided, and Tyndale fled up the river Rhine with whatever printed sheets he could save. In 1526 he succeeded in the city of Worms. And here is a lovely link to an earlier part of our story: the printer was Peter Schoeffer the Younger, son of the very Peter Schoeffer who had worked with Gutenberg and Fust in Mainz. The little pocket-sized New Testament, an octavo, was printed in perhaps 3,000 copies and smuggled into England hidden in bales of cloth and barrels of goods.

The Bishop of London, Cuthbert Tunstall, bought up copies and had them publicly burned. That simply gave Tyndale money to print more. Today only three copies of the 1526 Worms New Testament are known: one at the British Library, an incomplete one at St Paul's Cathedral in London, and one identified in 1996 in the State Library of Württemberg in Stuttgart, which is the most complete of the three.

Tyndale's story ended sadly. He was betrayed in Antwerp in 1535, imprisoned at Vilvoorde castle near Brussels, and executed for heresy in 1536. Yet his words lived on. Much of the wording of the famous King James Bible of 1611 comes directly from Tyndale's translation, including phrases English speakers still use, such as let there be light and the powers that be. A man who was hunted and killed for printing a book ended up shaping the English language for centuries.

sections.heading: Trying to Put the Genie Back in the Bottle
paragraphs: If you were a ruler or a bishop in the 1500s, the printing press could look frightening. For centuries the people in charge had been able to keep an eye on what was written, because books were few and copied slowly. Now a printer in a distant town could turn out a thousand copies of an angry pamphlet in a few days. Authorities on every side tried to get control back, and the main tools they used were censorship, licensing and lists of forbidden books.

Censorship means checking writing before or after it is published and stopping what the authorities do not like. Even before Luther, some church leaders had demanded that books be approved before printing. After 1517 the efforts grew much stronger. Lists of banned books appeared in the Catholic Netherlands in 1529, in Venice in 1543 and in Paris in 1551, where the theologians of the Sorbonne drew up their own catalogue.

In 1559 Pope Paul IV issued the first widely enforced Roman list, called the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, Latin for Index of Prohibited Books. It was extremely strict. It banned the entire works of about 550 authors, not just individual books, and it even included some Bibles printed in everyday languages. In 1564, after the great church meeting known as the Council of Trent, a revised and somewhat milder version, the Tridentine Index, set out rules that lasted for centuries. In 1571 a special group of church officials, the Congregation of the Index, was set up to examine new books and keep the list up to date.

Being on the Index meant that Catholics were forbidden to print, sell or read a book without special permission. Over the years it named works by many famous thinkers, including Galileo, Descartes, Voltaire and Kant. The list kept growing, and its last edition, in 1948, contained about 4,000 titles. It was finally abolished in 1966, when the church announced that it no longer had the force of church law. That means the Index lasted more than four centuries.

It would be unfair to suggest that only the Catholic Church censored. Protestant cities burned Catholic books and also banned the writings of other Protestant groups they disagreed with. Kings and city councils everywhere licensed printers, which meant you needed official permission to run a press at all. In England, the Stationers' Company, a guild of printers and booksellers in London, received a royal charter in 1557 that let it control most printing in the kingdom, and books had to be registered before they appeared.

Printers who broke the rules could lose everything. Their type and presses might be confiscated, their stock burned, and some were imprisoned or even executed. Many printers responded with tricks: false city names on title pages, no printer's name at all, or presses moved across the nearest border. Books printed in Geneva, Antwerp, Basel or later Amsterdam slipped into countries where they were forbidden. Censorship could slow ideas down and frighten people, but it never managed to stop print completely. A recurring lesson of this period is that once a text exists in hundreds of copies, it is very hard to make it disappear.

sections.heading: Copies You Can Trust: Science in Print
paragraphs: Now let us leave the religious arguments and step into the workshops of scientists, because printing changed science in a quieter but equally powerful way. To see why, imagine you are a scholar in 1400 studying an old book about the stars or the human body. Your copy was made by hand, and so was the copy it came from, and so on back for centuries. Every scribe made a few mistakes, especially with numbers and diagrams. Two scholars in different cities might be reading two quite different versions of the same book without knowing it.

Printing changed that. When a printer made 500 copies of a book, all 500 had the same words, the same numbers and the same pictures on the same pages. A professor in Padua could write to a professor in Kraków about the diagram on page 37, and both would be looking at the same diagram. If someone spotted an error, it could be listed and corrected in the next edition, and everyone could check. This sounds simple, but it made it far easier for scholars to build on each other's work and to argue about evidence.

Two famous books from the same year, 1543, show this new power. The first was by the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus. For many years he had worked out a startling idea: that the Earth and the other planets travel around the Sun, rather than everything circling a still Earth. He hesitated to publish, but a young mathematician named Georg Joachim Rheticus came to visit him, became his student, and encouraged him. The finished book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, was printed in Nuremberg by Johannes Petreius, one of the city's leading printers.

Copernicus died in May 1543, the same year his book was published. A traditional story says the first printed copy was placed in his hands on the very day he died. Nobody can prove that, so treat it as a touching legend. The book was not an instant best-seller. Its first print run of about 400 copies did not even sell out. But printed copies travelled, and astronomers filled the margins with notes. The historian Owen Gingerich spent decades tracking down surviving copies and found 276 copies of the first edition and 325 of the second, many covered with readers' handwriting, showing how carefully they were studied.

The second great book of 1543 was On the Fabric of the Human Body, by Andreas Vesalius, a 28-year-old professor of anatomy at the University of Padua. Unlike many teachers before him, Vesalius cut up human bodies himself to see what was really there instead of simply repeating the ancient Greek doctor Galen. He found that Galen, who had mostly dissected animals, was wrong about many details of human anatomy.

The Fabrica, as it is usually called, was a huge book printed in Basel, Switzerland, by Johannes Oporinus. Its real wonder was its pictures: more than 250 detailed woodcuts, drawn by skilled artists probably connected to the workshop of the famous Venetian painter Titian. The carved woodblocks were carried across the Alps from Italy to Basel. Its skeletons and muscle men stand in landscapes, as if posing for a portrait. Because every copy had exactly the same pictures, students across Europe could learn anatomy from the same accurate images, and other doctors could check them against real bodies. Vesalius also published a shorter, cheaper version, the Epitome, for students.

Some astronomers even became their own printers. The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe set up a printing press and a paper mill on his island observatory of Hven in the late 1500s so he could publish his observations exactly as he wanted them. That shows how much scientists had come to rely on print.

sections.heading: Maps, Tables and the Mathematics of the Sea
paragraphs: Science is not only words. It is full of numbers, tables, charts and maps, and these are precisely the things that hand-copying ruins most easily. Change one word in a poem and you might still understand it. Change one number in a table of star positions or tides and a ship might end up on the rocks.

In the age of ocean voyages, printed maps became hugely important. Many of the finest were printed from engraved copper plates, where the lines were cut into metal with a sharp tool, allowing much finer detail than woodcuts. In 1569 the Flemish mapmaker Gerard Mercator printed a giant world map using a new way of drawing the round Earth on a flat sheet. On his map, a course with a constant compass direction appears as a straight line, which made it extremely useful for sailors. The price was that lands far from the equator, like Greenland, look much bigger than they really are. Versions of the Mercator projection are still used on many online maps today.

A year later, on 20 May 1570, the Antwerp mapmaker Abraham Ortelius published the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum, the Theatre of the World, often called the first modern atlas. It gathered 53 maps of the same style and size into one book, so readers could compare regions easily. Ortelius listed the mapmakers he had copied from, which helped readers judge how reliable each map was, and he updated later editions as new information arrived. A printed atlas could be improved edition after edition, like a scientific report.

Printed mathematical tables were just as important. Navigators, astronomers, merchants and surveyors used tables of positions, distances and calculations. In 1614 the Scottish mathematician John Napier published his description of logarithms, a clever trick that turns long multiplications into simpler additions, along with tables of numbers. Printed tables of logarithms spread across Europe and saved people countless hours of calculating for more than 300 years, until electronic calculators took over.

Print could carry discoveries quickly too. In March 1610 the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei published a short book called the Starry Messenger, describing what he had seen through his telescope: mountains on the Moon, many more stars than anyone had counted and four moons circling Jupiter. Its print run of about 550 copies sold out quickly, and within months scholars across Europe were arguing about it and trying to build telescopes of their own.

But fixed copies had a funny downside: mistakes were copied perfectly too. In 1631 the royal printers in London produced a Bible in which the word not was missing from one of the Ten Commandments, so it read Thou shalt commit adultery. It became known as the Wicked Bible. The printers were heavily fined and most copies were destroyed. One tiny slip in the type became hundreds of identical errors, which is why careful proofreading became so important.

sections.heading: Did Printing Change Everything?
paragraphs: With so much happening at once, it is tempting to say the printing press caused the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution. Historians have argued about this for a long time, and the debate is a great example of how history really works.

In 1979 an American historian named Elizabeth Eisenstein published a big two-volume book called The Printing Press as an Agent of Change. She argued that historians had badly underrated print. Printing, she said, did three big things. It spread texts far more widely, which she called dissemination. It made copies identical, so that maps, numbers, spellings and pictures became standardized. And it preserved texts, because once hundreds of copies existed in many places, a book was very unlikely to be lost forever, as many ancient works had been. These changes, she argued, helped make the Reformation, the spread of Renaissance learning and the rise of modern science possible.

Notice that her title calls print an agent of change, not the only cause. Still, other historians pushed back. Some pointed out that early printed books were often full of mistakes, that pirate printers copied each other carelessly, and that different editions of the same book could differ. The historian Adrian Johns argued that trust in printed books had to be built up slowly by people, rules and reputations; it did not come automatically with the machine. Others noted that East Asia had printing for centuries before Europe, yet its history unfolded differently, so the press alone cannot explain what happened in Europe.

Most historians today take a middle position. The Reformation also needed Luther's ideas, the support of powerful princes, anger about money and power in the church, and changes in society. The Scientific Revolution needed observatories, universities, instruments like the telescope, and bold thinkers. Printing did not make these things happen by itself. But it acted like a powerful amplifier, a loudspeaker for ideas. It let arguments reach more people, faster, in more identical copies, than ever before, and it made it much harder for anyone to silence them completely.

By 1600 Europe was a very different place from the Europe of Gutenberg's youth. Religion had split into several churches. Scientists were comparing printed observations across countries. And millions of people who would never meet each other were reading the same words. The next question was what printing would do to everyday life itself: to news, language, the law and the farthest corners of the world.

deepDive: How much did print really matter to the Reformation? Historians have tried to answer with numbers. Surveys of surviving German imprints show a dramatic jump in output after 1517, peaking in the early 1520s and then dropping steeply after 1525. Most of the growth came from short vernacular pamphlets rather than big books. Andrew Pettegree counts about 828 editions of Luther's works by the end of 1522, and estimates that in 1521–1525 evangelical writers outpublished their Catholic opponents roughly nine to one. Yet literacy was low, perhaps a few percent in rural areas and higher in towns, so print worked together with sermons, songs, reading aloud and pictures. This is why many scholars describe a 'multimedia' Reformation rather than a purely printed one. The science side raises a different question. Elizabeth Eisenstein argued in 1979 that print's 'fixity' (identical copies), together with wider dissemination and safer preservation, allowed knowledge to accumulate instead of decaying with each hand copy. Her critics, notably Adrian Johns, replied that early print was anything but fixed: pirated editions, careless compositors and rival versions were everywhere, and trust in printed books had to be built socially, through printers' reputations, licensing, learned societies and errata lists. Owen Gingerich's census of Copernicus's book offers a neat test case: about 600 surviving copies of the first two editions, many heavily annotated, show readers copying corrections and notes from one another's copies, so that knowledge travelled partly through print and partly through handwriting in the margins. Comparisons with East Asia, where printing was far older but social and political conditions differed, also warn against treating the press as a single cause. The fairest summary is that print was a powerful amplifier and preserver, whose effects depended on who controlled it, who could read, and what people wanted to argue about.
funFact: Martin Luther, whose ideas spread thanks to printers, called the printing press "God's highest and most extreme act of grace."
